Lecture 14

Coupled oscillations and normal coordinates

We derive the equation Mq¨+Kq=fM\ddot{\vv q}+K\vv q=\vv fMq¨​+Kq=f for masses joined by springs and prove that a positive-definite mass matrix and a symmetric stiffness matrix give real eigenvalues and a basis of mode vectors that is orthonormal in the mass-weighted product. We then solve initial-value problems in normal coordinates, including a zero mode, and find the periodic response to a periodic force.

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

  • Derive the equation Mq¨+Kq=fM\ddot{\vv q}+K\vv q=\vv fMq¨​+Kq=f and its displacement–velocity system from the forces on the bodies.
  • Compute the eigenvalues and mass-orthonormal mode vectors of Kv=λMvK\vv v=\lambda M\vv vKv=λMv for a positive-definite MMM and a symmetric KKK.
  • Solve an initial-value problem in normal coordinates and check it against both the displacement and the velocity data.
  • Decide from KKK whether all modes oscillate, and interpret zero modes and the periodic response to a periodic force.

Lecture 9 studied one body on a spring. When several bodies are joined by springs, each one pushes and pulls its neighbours, and their displacements obey a system of second-order equations. In this lecture we derive this system from the forces and find the motions in which all bodies oscillate with one common frequency and fixed amplitude ratios. These normal modes come from an eigenvalue problem weighted by the masses. Unlike the modes of the tanks in Lecture 13, they can be chosen orthonormal in a mass-weighted product, and projections in that product give their coefficients. In the coordinates they define, the system splits into independent scalar oscillators, which Lectures 8 and 9 solve.

14.1 Masses joined by springs

As in Lectures 10–13, III is the identity matrix and JJJ an open interval of times. Figure 14.1 shows two bodies with the masses m1m_1m1​ and m2m_2m2​ on a frictionless floor. A spring with the constant k1k_1k1​ joins the first body to the left wall, a spring with the constant k2k_2k2​ joins the two bodies, and a spring with the constant k3k_3k3​ joins the second body to the right wall. The displacements q1q_1q1​ and q2q_2q2​ are measured from the positions in which no spring is stretched, and the external forces F1(t)F_1(t)F1​(t) and F2(t)F_2(t)F2​(t) act on the bodies.

By Hooke’s law a spring stretched by the length ddd pulls on each of its ends with the force kdkdkd towards its other end. The first spring is stretched by q1q_1q1​, the middle spring by q2−q1q_2-q_1q2​−q1​ and the last spring by −q2-q_2−q2​. Newton’s second law for each body gives m1q¨1=−k1q1+k2(q2−q1)+F1(t),m2q¨2=−k2(q2−q1)−k3q2+F2(t).\begin{aligned} m_1\ddot q_1&=-k_1q_1+k_2(q_2-q_1)+F_1(t),\\ m_2\ddot q_2&=-k_2(q_2-q_1)-k_3q_2+F_2(t). \end{aligned}m1​q¨​1​m2​q¨​2​​=−k1​q1​+k2​(q2​−q1​)+F1​(t),=−k2​(q2​−q1​)−k3​q2​+F2​(t).​(14.1) With q=(q1,q2)\vv q=(q_1,q_2)q=(q1​,q2​) and f=(F1,F2)\vv f=(F_1,F_2)f=(F1​,F2​) this is Mq¨+Kq=fM\ddot{\vv q}+K\vv q=\vv fMq¨​+Kq=f, where M=(m100m2),K=(k1+k2−k2−k2k2+k3).M=\begin{pmatrix}m_1&0\\0&m_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad K=\begin{pmatrix}k_1+k_2&-k_2\\-k_2&k_2+k_3\end{pmatrix}.M=(m1​0​0m2​​),K=(k1​+k2​−k2​​−k2​k2​+k3​​).(14.2) The matrix KKK is symmetric. Its off-diagonal entries are equal because the middle spring pulls on both bodies with forces of equal size and opposite directions. The potential energy stored in the springs is V=12k1q12+12k2(q2−q1)2+12k3q22=12qTKq,V=\frac12k_1q_1^2+\frac12k_2(q_2-q_1)^2+\frac12k_3q_2^2=\frac12\vv q^{\T}K\vv q,V=21​k1​q12​+21​k2​(q2​−q1​)2+21​k3​q22​=21​qTKq, and the spring forces are the components of −Kq-K\vv q−Kq. The same construction applies to nnn bodies on a line, with an n×nn\times nn×n diagonal matrix MMM and a symmetric matrix KKK. Other coordinates, for example angles, give matrices MMM that are not diagonal (Riley, Hobson and Bence, §9.1, whose kinetic and potential matrices are 12M\tfrac12M21​M and 12K\tfrac12K21​K). The properties we use are the following.

m1q¨1=−k1q1+k2(q2−q1)+F1(t),m2q¨2=−k2(q2−q1)−k3q2+F2(t).\begin{aligned} m_1\ddot q_1&=-k_1q_1+k_2(q_2-q_1)+F_1(t),\\ m_2\ddot q_2&=-k_2(q_2-q_1)-k_3q_2+F_2(t). \end{aligned}m1​q¨​1​m2​q¨​2​​=−k1​q1​+k2​(q2​−q1​)+F1​(t),=−k2​(q2​−q1​)−k3​q2​+F2​(t).​(14.1)
M=(m100m2),K=(k1+k2−k2−k2k2+k3).M=\begin{pmatrix}m_1&0\\0&m_2\end{pmatrix},\qquad K=\begin{pmatrix}k_1+k_2&-k_2\\-k_2&k_2+k_3\end{pmatrix}.M=(m1​0​0m2​​),K=(k1​+k2​−k2​​−k2​k2​+k3​​).(14.2)

Definition 14.1 (Mass and stiffness matrices). A real symmetric n×nn\times nn×n matrix SSS is positive definite if qTSq>0\vv q^{\T}S\vv q>0qTSq>0 for every nonzero q∈Rn\vv q\in\R^nq∈Rn. The equation of coupled linear oscillators is Mq¨+Kq=f(t),M\ddot{\vv q}+K\vv q=\vv f(t),Mq¨​+Kq=f(t),(14.3) where the mass matrix MMM is real symmetric and positive definite, the stiffness matrix KKK is real symmetric, and the force f\vv ff is continuous on JJJ with values in Rn\R^nRn.

The diagonal matrix MMM of (14.2) is positive definite, because qTMq=m1q12+m2q22\vv q^{\T}M\vv q=m_1q_1^2+m_2q_2^2qTMq=m1​q12​+m2​q22​. The matrix KKK of (14.2) is positive definite when k1k_1k1​, k2k_2k2​ and k3k_3k3​ are positive. Indeed, VVV is a sum of three nonnegative terms, so V=0V=0V=0 forces each term to vanish, that is, q1=0q_1=0q1​=0 and q2=0q_2=0q2​=0. Without the walls, that is, for k1=k3=0k_1=k_3=0k1​=k3​=0, the energy V=12k2(q2−q1)2V=\tfrac12k_2(q_2-q_1)^2V=21​k2​(q2​−q1​)2 vanishes for q1=q2≠0q_1=q_2\ne0q1​=q2​=0, and KKK is not positive definite.

Proposition 14.2 (Energy). Let q\vv qq solve (14.3) on JJJ. The energy E=12q˙TMq˙+12qTKqE=\tfrac12\dot{\vv q}^{\T}M\dot{\vv q}+\tfrac12\vv q^{\T}K\vv qE=21​q˙​TMq˙​+21​qTKq satisfies E˙=q˙Tf\dot E=\dot{\vv q}^{\T}\vv fE˙=q˙​Tf. In particular, EEE is constant when f=0\vv f=0f=0.

Proof. Hence E˙=q˙TMq¨+q˙TKq=q˙T(Mq¨+Kq)=q˙Tf.\dot E=\dot{\vv q}^{\T}M\ddot{\vv q}+\dot{\vv q}^{\T}K\vv q =\dot{\vv q}^{\T}\bigl(M\ddot{\vv q}+K\vv q\bigr)=\dot{\vv q}^{\T}\vv f.E˙=q˙​TMq¨​+q˙​TKq=q˙​T(Mq¨​+Kq)=q˙​Tf.■

14.3 Normal modes

We look for motions q(t)=vcos⁡(ωt)\vv q(t)=\vv v\cos(\omega t)q(t)=vcos(ωt) of (14.3) with f=0\vv f=0f=0, in which all bodies oscillate with one frequency and the fixed amplitude ratios given by v\vv vv. Substitution gives (K−ω2M)vcos⁡(ωt)=0(K-\omega^2M)\vv v\cos(\omega t)=0(K−ω2M)vcos(ωt)=0, so Kv=ω2MvK\vv v=\omega^2M\vv vKv=ω2Mv.

Definition 14.3 (Generalized eigenvalue problem). Let MMM and KKK be as in Definition 14.1. A number λ∈C\lambda\in\Cλ∈C is an eigenvalue of KKK relative to MMM with the mode vector v∈Cn\vv v\in\C^nv∈Cn if v≠0\vv v\ne0v=0 and Kv=λMv.K\vv v=\lambda M\vv v.Kv=λMv.(14.5)

Since MMM is invertible, (14.5) says M−1Kv=λvM^{-1}K\vv v=\lambda\vv vM−1Kv=λv. So the eigenvalues relative to MMM are the eigenvalues of M−1KM^{-1}KM−1K, the roots of det⁡(K−λM)=det⁡M det⁡(M−1K−λI)\det(K-\lambda M)=\det M\,\det(M^{-1}K-\lambda I)det(K−λM)=detMdet(M−1K−λI). There are nnn of them, counted with multiplicity. The matrix M−1KM^{-1}KM−1K is not symmetric in general, so the spectral theorem for symmetric matrices does not apply to it directly. We use a different inner product instead. For y\vv yy and w\vv ww in Rn\R^nRn let ⟨y,w⟩M=yTMw.\inner{\vv y}{\vv w}_M=\vv y^{\T}M\vv w.⟨y,w⟩M​=yTMw.(14.6)

⟨y,w⟩M=yTMw.\inner{\vv y}{\vv w}_M=\vv y^{\T}M\vv w.⟨y,w⟩M​=yTMw.(14.6)

Theorem 14.4 (Mode vectors). Let MMM be real symmetric and positive definite and KKK real symmetric.

  • Every eigenvalue of KKK relative to MMM is real.

  • Mode vectors v\vv vv and w\vv ww for different eigenvalues satisfy vTMw=0\vv v^{\T}M\vv w=0vTMw=0.

  • There is a basis v1,…,vn\vv v_1,\dots,\vv v_nv1​,…,vn​ of Rn\R^nRn of mode vectors, Kvj=λjMvjK\vv v_j=\lambda_jM\vv v_jKvj​=λj​Mvj​, with viTMvj=δijandviTKvj=λjδij.\vv v_i^{\T}M\vv v_j=\delta_{ij}\qquad\text{and}\qquad \vv v_i^{\T}K\vv v_j=\lambda_j\delta_{ij}.viT​Mvj​=δij​andviT​Kvj​=λj​δij​.(14.7)

  • All λj\lambda_jλj​ are positive if and only if KKK is positive definite.

Proof. First, let Kv=λMvK\vv v=\lambda M\vv vKv=λMv with a nonzero v∈Cn\vv v\in\C^nv∈Cn, and write v=a+ib\vv v=\vv a+\iu\vv bv=a+ib with real a\vv aa and b\vv bb. Multiplying by v†=aT−ibT\vv v^{\adj}=\vv a^{\T}-\iu\vv b^{\T}v†=aT−ibT gives v†Kv=λ v†Mv\vv v^{\adj}K\vv v=\lambda\,\vv v^{\adj}M\vv vv†Kv=λv†Mv. For a real symmetric SSS the cross terms cancel, because aTSb=bTSa\vv a^{\T}S\vv b=\vv b^{\T}S\vv aaTSb=bTSa: v†Sv=aTSa+bTSb+i(aTSb−bTSa)=aTSa+bTSb.\vv v^{\adj}S\vv v=\vv a^{\T}S\vv a+\vv b^{\T}S\vv b+\iu\bigl(\vv a^{\T}S\vv b-\vv b^{\T}S\vv a\bigr) =\vv a^{\T}S\vv a+\vv b^{\T}S\vv b.v†Sv=aTSa+bTSb+i(aTSb−bTSa)=aTSa+bTSb. We apply this to S=KS=KS=K and to S=MS=MS=M. So v†Kv\vv v^{\adj}K\vv vv†Kv is real, and v†Mv>0\vv v^{\adj}M\vv v>0v†Mv>0 since a\vv aa and b\vv bb are not both zero. Hence λ=v†Kv/v†Mv\lambda=\vv v^{\adj}K\vv v/\vv v^{\adj}M\vv vλ=v†Kv/v†Mv is real.

Next, let Kv=λMvK\vv v=\lambda M\vv vKv=λMv and Kw=λ′MwK\vv w=\lambda'M\vv wKw=λ′Mw with λ≠λ′\lambda\ne\lambda'λ=λ′. By the symmetry of KKK and MMM, λ′ vTMw=vTKw=(Kv)Tw=λ vTMw,\lambda'\,\vv v^{\T}M\vv w=\vv v^{\T}K\vv w=(K\vv v)^{\T}\vv w=\lambda\,\vv v^{\T}M\vv w,λ′vTMw=vTKw=(Kv)Tw=λvTMw, so (λ′−λ) vTMw=0(\lambda'-\lambda)\,\vv v^{\T}M\vv w=0(λ′−λ)vTMw=0 and vTMw=0\vv v^{\T}M\vv w=0vTMw=0.

Then, (14.6) is an inner product on Rn\R^nRn: it is linear in each slot, symmetric because MMM is symmetric, and positive definite because MMM is. A real inner product is exactly such a form (LA 7, Definition “Inner product, physics convention”, and the paragraph after it). An operator GGG on a space with an inner product ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}⟨⋅,⋅⟩ is self-adjoint if ⟨y,Gw⟩=⟨Gy,w⟩\inner{\vv y}{G\vv w}=\inner{G\vv y}{\vv w}⟨y,Gw⟩=⟨Gy,w⟩ for all y\vv yy and w\vv ww (LA 9, Definition “Self-adjoint operator”). Let GGG be the operator on Rn\R^nRn given by Gw=M−1KwG\vv w=M^{-1}K\vv wGw=M−1Kw. Then ⟨y,Gw⟩M=yTKw=(Ky)Tw=(MGy)Tw=⟨Gy,w⟩M,\inner{\vv y}{G\vv w}_M=\vv y^{\T}K\vv w=(K\vv y)^{\T}\vv w=(MG\vv y)^{\T}\vv w =\inner{G\vv y}{\vv w}_M,⟨y,Gw⟩M​=yTKw=(Ky)Tw=(MGy)Tw=⟨Gy,w⟩M​, so GGG is self-adjoint for ⟨⋅,⋅⟩M\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_M⟨⋅,⋅⟩M​. By the spectral theorem (LA 10, Theorem “Spectral theorem for self-adjoint operators”, which covers real spaces) Rn\R^nRn has a basis v1,…,vn\vv v_1,\dots,\vv v_nv1​,…,vn​ that is orthonormal for ⟨⋅,⋅⟩M\inner{\cdot}{\cdot}_M⟨⋅,⋅⟩M​ and consists of eigenvectors of GGG. These are mode vectors, and orthonormality is viTMvj=δij\vv v_i^{\T}M\vv v_j=\delta_{ij}viT​Mvj​=δij​. Then viTKvj=λjviTMvj=λjδij\vv v_i^{\T}K\vv v_j=\lambda_j\vv v_i^{\T}M\vv v_j=\lambda_j\delta_{ij}viT​Kvj​=λj​viT​Mvj​=λj​δij​.

Finally, write q=∑jcjvj\vv q=\sum_jc_j\vv v_jq=∑j​cj​vj​. By (14.7), qTKq=∑jλjcj2\vv q^{\T}K\vv q=\sum_j\lambda_jc_j^2qTKq=∑j​λj​cj2​. If all λj>0\lambda_j>0λj​>0, this is positive for q≠0\vv q\ne0q=0. Conversely, if KKK is positive definite, then λj=vjTKvj>0\lambda_j=\vv v_j^{\T}K\vv v_j>0λj​=vjT​Kvj​>0. ■

The orthogonality vTMw=0\vv v^{\T}M\vv w=0vTMw=0 of mode vectors for different eigenvalues is the mass-weighted orthogonality. The mode vectors are in general not orthogonal in the ordinary sense, and the example of Section 14.6 shows this. In the language of Lecture 13, the vj\vv v_jvj​ are right eigenvectors of M−1KM^{-1}KM−1K, and the MvjM\vv v_jMvj​ are left eigenvectors, because (Mvj)TM−1K=vjTK=λj(Mvj)T(M\vv v_j)^{\T}M^{-1}K=\vv v_j^{\T}K=\lambda_j(M\vv v_j)^{\T}(Mvj​)TM−1K=vjT​K=λj​(Mvj​)T. The normalization ℓi†vj=δij\vv\ell_i^{\adj}\vv v_j=\delta_{ij}ℓi†​vj​=δij​ of Lecture 13, with ℓi=Mvi\vv\ell_i=M\vv v_iℓi​=Mvi​, is (14.7). Another route uses the symmetric matrix M−1/2KM−1/2M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}M−1/2KM−1/2. For a diagonal MMM the matrix M−1/2M^{-1/2}M−1/2 is diag⁡(1/m1,…,1/mn)\diag(1/\sqrt{m_1},\dots,1/\sqrt{m_n})diag(1/m1​​,…,1/mn​​), and for a general MMM it is built from the spectral theorem for MMM. We do not need it.

14.4 Normal coordinates

With the basis of the theorem, every displacement is a combination of mode vectors, and the coefficients are computed with the mass-weighted product.

Definition 14.5 (Normal coordinates and normal modes). Let v1,…,vn\vv v_1,\dots,\vv v_nv1​,…,vn​ be a basis as in Theorem 14.4. The normal coordinates of a function q(t)\vv q(t)q(t) are ηj(t)=vjTMq(t),j=1,…,n.\eta_j(t)=\vv v_j^{\T}M\vv q(t),\qquad j=1,\dots,n.ηj​(t)=vjT​Mq(t),j=1,…,n.(14.8) A normal mode is a solution of (14.3) with f=0\vv f=0f=0 in which only one normal coordinate is not identically zero. For λj>0\lambda_j>0λj​>0 the number ωj=λj\omega_j=\sqrt{\lambda_j}ωj​=λj​​ is a normal frequency.

By the expansion in an orthonormal basis (LA 8, Theorem “Expansion in an orthonormal basis”), applied to the inner product (14.6), q(t)=∑j=1nηj(t) vj.\vv q(t)=\sum_{j=1}^n\eta_j(t)\,\vv v_j.q(t)=j=1∑n​ηj​(t)vj​.(14.9)

q(t)=∑j=1nηj(t) vj.\vv q(t)=\sum_{j=1}^n\eta_j(t)\,\vv v_j.q(t)=j=1∑n​ηj​(t)vj​.(14.9)

Theorem 14.6 (Solution in normal coordinates). Let MMM, KKK, vj\vv v_jvj​ and λj\lambda_jλj​ be as in Theorem 14.4, let f\vv ff be continuous on JJJ, let t0∈Jt_0\in Jt0​∈J, and let q0\vv q_0q0​ and u0\vv u_0u0​ be in Rn\R^nRn. Proposition 14.7 (Stability of coupled oscillators). Let f=0\vv f=0f=0. The system (14.4) is stable in the sense of Lecture 12 if and only if KKK is positive definite. It is never asymptotically stable.

The response is large near either normal frequency, because the force drives both modes. Between them, at ω2=12(ω12+ω22)=(k+kc)/m\omega^2=\tfrac12(\omega_1^2+\omega_2^2)=(k+k_{\mathrm c})/mω2=21​(ω12​+ω22​)=(k+kc​)/m, the driven body does not move in this periodic solution, and the second body moves with qp,2=−(F0/kc)cos⁡ωtq_{\mathrm p,2}=-(F_0/k_{\mathrm c})\cos\omega tqp,2​=−(F0​/kc​)cosωt. This agrees with the forces on the first body. At rest it feels the drive F0cos⁡ωtF_0\cos\omega tF0​cosωt and the middle spring kcqp,2k_{\mathrm c}q_{\mathrm p,2}kc​qp,2​, and these cancel. The frequency (k+kc)/m\sqrt{(k+k_{\mathrm c})/m}(k+kc​)/m​ is that of the second body when the first is held fixed. A vibration absorber uses this effect. A second body tuned in this way keeps a driven part still.

By linearity, q−qp\vv q-\vv q_{\mathrm p}q−qp​ solves the equation with f=0\vv f=0f=0 for every solution q\vv qq. So every solution is qp\vv q_{\mathrm p}qp​ plus a free motion, which the data fix. Without damping a nonzero free motion does not decay, unlike the transient of Lecture 9. ◃

14.6 A free molecule

Without the walls the stiffness matrix is not positive definite. A diatomic molecule moving along its axis is the simplest example. It also shows unequal masses.

Example 14.10 (A struck diatomic molecule). We find the motion of two atoms after one of them is struck. The atoms have the masses m1m_1m1​ and m2m_2m2​ and are joined by a bond that acts as a spring with the constant kkk. At t=0t=0t=0 both are at rest at their equilibrium positions, and a blow gives the first atom the velocity u>0u>0u>0 towards the second atom, which lies to its right. By (14.12) the kinetic energy 12m1u2\tfrac12m_1u^221​m1​u2 of the blow splits into 12η˙1(0)2=12(m1+m2)(m1u/(m1+m2))2\tfrac12\dot\eta_1(0)^2=\tfrac12(m_1+m_2)\bigl(m_1u/(m_1+m_2)\bigr)^221​η˙​1​(0)2=21​(m1​+m2​)(m1​u/(m1​+m2​))2 for the drift and 12η˙2(0)2=12u2m1m2/(m1+m2)\tfrac12\dot\eta_2(0)^2=\tfrac12u^2m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)21​η˙​2​(0)2=21​u2m1​m2​/(m1​+m2​) for the vibration. ◃

The zero mode is the free motion of the whole molecule. It makes the system unstable in the sense of Lecture 12. The bond length stays bounded, and only the position of the molecule grows.

Summary

Masses joined by springs obey Mq¨+Kq=fM\ddot{\vv q}+K\vv q=\vv fMq¨​+Kq=f, with a positive-definite mass matrix and a symmetric stiffness matrix. The initial data are the nnn displacements and the nnn velocities. The eigenvalues of KKK relative to MMM are real, and the mode vectors can be chosen orthonormal in the mass-weighted product yTMw\vv y^{\T}M\vv wyTMw. The normal coordinates ηj=vjTMq\eta_j=\vv v_j^{\T}M\vv qηj​=vjT​Mq satisfy independent scalar equations η¨j+λjηj=vjTf\ddot\eta_j+\lambda_j\eta_j=\vv v_j^{\T}\vv fη¨​j​+λj​ηj​=vjT​f, with data computed by the same product. All modes oscillate exactly when KKK is positive definite. A zero eigenvalue gives a uniform motion, and a negative one gives exponentially growing solutions. In free motion each mode keeps its energy, while the energy can move between the bodies, as in beats.

  • Model: Mq¨+Kq=fM\ddot{\vv q}+K\vv q=\vv fMq¨​+Kq=f, MMM symmetric positive definite, KKK symmetric; energy 12q˙TMq˙+12qTKq\tfrac12\dot{\vv q}^{\T}M\dot{\vv q}+\tfrac12\vv q^{\T}K\vv q21​q˙​TMq˙​+21​qTKq.

  • Mode vectors: Kvj=λjMvjK\vv v_j=\lambda_jM\vv v_jKvj​=λj​Mvj​ with real λj\lambda_jλj​; a basis with viTMvj=δij\vv v_i^{\T}M\vv v_j=\delta_{ij}viT​Mvj​=δij​ and viTKvj=λjδij\vv v_i^{\T}K\vv v_j=\lambda_j\delta_{ij}viT​Kvj​=λj​δij​.

  • Normal coordinates: ηj=vjTMq\eta_j=\vv v_j^{\T}M\vv qηj​=vjT​Mq, q=∑jηjvj\vv q=\sum_j\eta_j\vv v_jq=∑j​ηj​vj​, η¨j+λjηj=vjTf\ddot\eta_j+\lambda_j\eta_j=\vv v_j^{\T}\vv fη¨​j​+λj​ηj​=vjT​f.

  • Oscillation: all λj=ωj2>0\lambda_j=\omega_j^2>0λj​=ωj2​>0 if and only if KKK is positive definite; then every free motion is bounded and no nonzero free motion tends to 000.

This lecture closes Part I. Lecture 15 begins Part II with complex differentiability and analytic functions, whose real parts are harmonic functions in the plane; locally these include the logarithm of the radius in Lecture 2.
